reply: I lifted a big pot plant on Saturday and felt a twinge. By Sunday, I could barely get out of bed. The pain is low on the left side of my back and sometimes goes into my left buttock. It gets worse when I bend or get up from a chair, but it's better when I lie still with a heat pack. It's worse in the evening, but I've been working from home the last two days, mostly lying on the couch with the laptop. I can walk around slowly.

utterance:
I've examined your back and your legs. This looks like a muscle strain in the lower back from lifting the pot plant — the muscles on the left are tight and sore, but the nerves to your legs are working normally. There's no sign of a slipped disc pressing on a nerve, and nothing worrying like infection or a problem with the nerves that control your bladder and bowels.

An MRI isn't needed right now. In the first few weeks after this kind of injury, a scan almost never changes what we do, and it often shows wear-and-tear changes that aren't the cause of the pain and can worry people unnecessarily. We'd only arrange a scan if the pain wasn't settling after about six weeks, or if warning signs appeared.

What helps most is staying gently active rather than lying on the couch all day. Short walks, changing position often, and heat packs are good. Avoid heavy lifting and deep bending for the next week or two, then build back up. You can work from a chair for short stretches with regular stand-and-stretch breaks — lying all day tends to stiffen things up.

I've prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg, one tablet three times a day with food, for up to a week. It reduces the inflammation and pain better than paracetamol alone. Because you have asthma, stop it and see me or go to emergency if you get wheeze, chest tightness, or trouble breathing. Also stop if you get stomach pain, black stools, or a rash. I've also given paracetamol 1 gram — that's two 500 mg tablets — up to four times a day if you still need extra relief. Don't take more than that, and you can use them together.

I've referred you to a physiotherapist. They can help with movement, pacing, and getting you back to normal faster. Please book in over the next few days.

Please come back sooner, or go to an emergency department straight away, if you get numbness around your groin or bottom, trouble passing urine or loss of bladder or bowel control, weakness in a leg, pain shooting below the knee, fever, or pain that is rapidly getting worse. If things aren't clearly improving in one to two weeks, come back and we'll review. Most people with this are much better within a few weeks. Do you have any questions?
reply: Honestly? I've been reading about slipped discs and people needing surgery.

awards.label: What he is worried the pain might be

utterance: It's understandable to worry after reading that. A slipped disc usually causes pain that shoots down the leg past the knee, often with tingling or weakness, and we didn't find those signs today. Even when someone does have a disc problem, the vast majority get better with time, movement, and simple pain relief — surgery is only for a small number who have severe nerve pressure that isn't improving, or an emergency like loss of bladder control. What you have fits a muscle strain, which is painful but not dangerous, and it should settle without an operation. Is there anything else you'd like me to go over?
reply: I just want to know what's going on. I'm worried it's serious.

utterance: What's going on is a strained muscle and some spasm on the left side of your lower back from the lift. It hurts a lot when you move because those muscles are guarding, which is why lying still feels better — but it is not a sign of something serious. Your examination is reassuring: normal strength, normal feeling in the legs, no nerve stretch pain, no fever, and no bladder or bowel warning signs. Serious causes are uncommon, and we've specifically looked for them. You should start to feel a bit better over the next few days with the anti-inflammatory, heat, and gentle movement, and most people are largely back to normal within two to four weeks. You're welcome to come back if you're still worried or not improving. Take care, Daniel.
reply: I just want to make sure I'm not missing something. I'm still a bit anxious about it being serious.

awards.label: Reasonable differential: Acute non-specific low back pain
Can't-miss diagnosis considered: Cauda equina syndrome

utterance: I hear that you're anxious, and that's a normal reaction when pain is this limiting. Based on how it started, the pattern of the pain, and today's examination, there isn't a sign we've missed of a serious cause. The plan is safe: anti-inflammatory with food, paracetamol if needed, gentle activity, physio, and a clear list of warning signs that mean you should get urgent care — groin numbness, trouble with bladder or bowels, leg weakness, fever, or rapidly worsening pain. If none of those appear and you're not improving in a week or two, come back and we'll reassess together. You don't need a scan today.
reply: I just want to be sure I'm doing everything right. I'm following the plan, but I'm still worried it might not be enough.
